#8561. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

First Highline on Trango Tower: On August 17, Lukas Irmler and Antonia Ruede-Passul of Germany completed the first-ever highline walk on Trango Towers in Pakistan’s Karakoram. They climbed Great Trango Tower to acclimatize before tackling Nameless Tower.

Setting up the 21m highline required fixed ropes and two summit ascents of Nameless Tower. The successful crossing saw Ruede-Passul break her own women’s highline altitude world record, previously set at 5,860m on Ojos de Salado in Chile, while Irmler surpassed 6,000m for the first time.

Following in the footsteps of Norway’s Great Adventurers: Steffen Skjottelvik set out to cross Canada, by foot, dog sled, and canoe, accompanied only by his beloved sled dogs. The Norwegian began his journey in 2023, but when one dog fell ill, he paused in the remote Cree community of Peawanuck. Here he found his home and a way of life that fitted him perfectly. He also fell in love with a local woman and became a second son to the community elders.

His original plan to travel by sled across the Hudson Bay coast changed after wolves killed one of his lead dogs. He decided to canoe the coastline in summer instead.

In 2025, he set off with his malamute Togo and a husky named Bay, facing polar bears, powerful tides, dense bogs, clouds of biting flies, and river crossings. On August 15, exhausted after weeks of difficult travel, Steffen could finally see his endpoint — the town of York Factory across the Hayes River. All he had to do was cross it. Togo survived and made it to shore, but Steffen’s body was found downstream 10 days later.

Where Was ‘Tenzing’ Filmed? Apple TV’s Tenzing recreates the historic 1953 first ascent of Everest, this time with Sherpa Tenzing Norgay at the center of the story. The filmmakers used real alpine environments across Nepal and New Zealand rather than green screens.

Nepal provided locations for Tenzing’s early life in the Lower Mustang, as well as the scenes in Darjeeling, Kathmandu, and Everest Base Camp. New Zealand’s Southern Alps, particularly the Aoraki region, doubled for Everest’s glaciers and icefalls, with the Darwin Icefall standing in for the notorious Khumbu Icefall.

Photographer Encounters Magnificent White Stag: Wildlife photographer Brian Johnston has captured incredible images of a rare white stag, believed to be an albino red deer. Johnston and a friend spotted the stag one windy morning during the rutting season, but it detected them and ran off.

Returning the following day, they found it asleep in a field, apparently exhausted after a night of rutting activity. Eventually, it stood up, giving Johnston the opportunity to photograph it.

Shark Attack Survivor Recounts Losing His Leg While Surfing: Australian firefighter and surfer Mel Ismail was surfing at Glenfield Beach on Australia’s west coast on September 14, when he was attacked by a shark. Sitting beyond the breaking waves, watching a pod of dolphins, Ismail initially thought a dolphin had bumped into his leg. Suddenly, he was dragged underwater and realized what was happening.

He desperately tried to push his fingers into the shark’s large black eye, and it released him. Ismail was bleeding heavily but managed to catch a wave toward shore. Another surfer spotted him and helped him onto the beach. Despite losing his leg below the knee, Ismail is determined to return to the water and start bodyboarding as soon as he can.

Canoe Dig It: Sam Dunning discovered freestyle canoeing during the 2020 lockdown after seeing a video of master paddler Marc Ornstein performing an interpretive routine to music. Amazed by the combination of technical skill and on-water choreography, the New York-based actor and filmmaker began writing Canoe Dig It?, a mockumentary inspired by comedies such as This Is Spinal Tap.

Winning the paddling community’s support was not easy, but at a freestyle canoeing symposium in Ohio, Dunning eventually met Ornstein. Ornstein and his wife agreed to be stunt doubles for the film.

Into Thin Air: This is a good background to the stories we’ve done on Kalie McCrystal, the 38-year-old skyrunner who disappeared on the Matterhorn on September 1. She met a Polish climber on her ascent, and theirs is the last footage of her. It shows her climbing towards the 4,478m summit. Shortly afterward, she was spotted descending the Italian side. Then she vanished.

Mountain rescuers believe she fell between 4,100m and 4,250m, but cannot establish exactly where or in which direction she fell. Despite a thorough search, no clothing, blood, or remains have been found. Her mother and sister eventually accepted that she had died on the mountain.

Climber Awarded Carnegie Medal After Rescuing Hang Glider Pilot: Matthew Clark has been awarded the Carnegie Medal for rescuing a hang glider pilot who crashed into a cliff on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

Clark, a 24-year-old climber and paraglider, had launched from the same spot minutes apart. Clark had just landed when he heard the crash reported over his radio. Reaching the scene with other pilots, he found Parson suspended in his harness around 15m above the ground.

With no walkable route to him, Clark spotted a narrow chimney nearby and free soloed up it, reaching him in about five minutes. Clark cut Parson free, moved him to safer ground, dressed a gash on his knee, and waited with him until a helicopter team was able to extract him on a long line.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8560. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:30 pm

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

Okay but with all that aside: I think I’ll always stay all-stock. Because volatility is only a problem for people who worry about fluctuating prices – the odds are still in your favor with an all-stock portfolio even when you are getting old.

Also note that if you own a house with no mortgage, that’s pretty big form of inflation-adjusted bond right there because it kicks out the equivalent of a rent payment that never goes up. And the principal portion (the value of your home) also keeps up with inflation which you can always cash out in the future if you change your mind or need to pay for long-term care or leave a big estate.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

Early in my career as a self-employed contractor, I would call up my buddy regularly to worry aloud how would I ever have enough work to feed my growing family.

This fear was valid. If I wanted them to eat, I had to buy food. If I wanted to buy food I needed money. To get money I needed paid work. To get paid work I had to sell jobs.

My buddy eventually reminded me that in between calling him up to worry aloud about not having enough work, I would also call him up regularly to beg him to help me with all the work I suddenly had lined up and now I wasn’t sure how I would get it all done!

Until he put it to me that way, I was too caught up in the moment to realize what I had been doing.

So, which is it? Are we afraid of not having enough? Or are we afraid of having too much?

Let’s not be afraid of either one. Either way, we are adaptable, capable and full of badassity!

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:24 pm

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

#8559. Order Takeout Direct and Pick It Up – Skip the App’s Markup & Fees

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Place takeout orders on the restaurant’s own website or app, then pick them up. On a delivery app, a menu markup, a service fee, a delivery fee, and a tip can add a third or more to the food’s price. Pay for a delivery membership only if your delivery fees come to more than $10 a month.

Part of that extra cost is in the menu prices, not the fees. Restaurants pay the apps a commission on each delivery order, 15% to 30% of the subtotal on DoorDash’s published plans, and DoorDash says many set different prices for delivery.

Say a restaurant lists a $36 dinner at $40 on the app, the app charges a 15% service fee and a $2 delivery fee, and you tip the driver 15%. With a $6 service fee and a $6 tip, that’s $54 before tax. Picked up from the restaurant at its own prices, the same dinner costs $36 before tax, so delivery through the app costs $18 more, half the food’s price.

That 15% is DoorDash’s service fee on most orders in California, Chicago, New York City, and six other places. Elsewhere, DoorDash is moving to a fee based on distance and order size. It can also add a fee to small orders. Uber Eats charges delivery and service fees too. Grubhub drops both on restaurant orders over $50, but any markup and the tip remain.

To pay the restaurant’s own prices, order on its website or app, or by phone, and pick it up. Join its rewards program, if it has one, so the order earns points. In an app, switching to pickup drops the delivery fee and the tip, and DoorDash’s terms for restaurants call for pickup prices to match in-store prices.

A delivery membership saves money only on deliveries you’d order anyway. DashPass and Uber One each cost $9.99 a month or $96 a year and waive the delivery fee and cut the service fee on eligible orders over a set minimum. If your delivery fees on such orders came to more than $10 last month, waiving them alone would have covered the $9.99 monthly price. Check whether you carry one of the credit cards that include DashPass before you pay for it.

On your next order, open the restaurant’s own site, price the same meal for pickup, and compare that total with the app’s.

#8558. Forgotten 7,000'ers: Changtse

Changtse is a rarely climbed peak in Tibet in the Everest massif, flanked by the Main Rongbuk and East Rongbuk Glaciers, and linked to the world’s highest mountain by the North Col. With a prominence of only 497m, Changtse is subordinate to its parent peak.

Modern Chinese mapping lists Changtse at 7,543m, though older sources cite figures up to 7,583m. The Changtse Glacier flows north into the East Rongbuk system, and some geographic surveys note a glacial lake on the glacier near 6,216m, ranking it among the world’s highest.

Because of Changtse’s connection to the classic northern approach to Everest, early mountaineering parties repeatedly crossed its flanks long before treating it as an independent objective.

In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine became the first climbers to set foot on Changtse. They climbed the East Ridge while scouting camp locations during the British Everest expedition.

During the 1935 British Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition led by Eric Shipton, the team divided to scout possible climbs before targeting Changtse. Bill Tilman and Edmund Wigram considered the peak’s Northwest Ridge but deemed it impracticable and crossed north of Changtse to Camp 2.

Meanwhile, Michael Spender and Charles Warren established high-altitude survey stations, and Shipton and Dan Bryant explored the West Rongbuk Glacier. Shipton’s primary goals were to photograph Everest’s upper sections and gather data on monsoon snow behavior. Despite deteriorating weather and waist-deep snow, they established three high camps.

On August 21, 1935, Shipton, Tilman, Wigram, Bryant, and Warren launched an attempt on Changtse. They climbed to within 460m of the summit before dangerously deep, soft monsoon snow forced them back. They spent a freezing night at high camp. Then, confronted by unstable slopes and buried tents, they abandoned their summit attempt.

Moving down the East Rongbuk Glacier on August 23, the climbers reunited with Spender, who had completed his difficult survey work, and headed toward the Kharta Changri Pass.

Base Camp of the 1924 Everest expedition. Photo: Royal Geographic Society

In 1952, during the British Cho Oyu Expedition, Edmund Hillary, George Lowe, and three Sherpas illegally crossed the Nup La Pass into Chinese-controlled Tibet after abandoning their Cho Oyu climb.

The group traveled to the North Side of Everest, exploring the East Rongbuk Glacier and visiting pre-war British base camp sites. Subsequently, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier for a direct attempt on Changtse’s summit. They reached 6,600m before a lack of food and supplies forced them to turn back. They returned over the pass to meet up with Shipton.

On October 3, 1982, Dutch climber Johan Taks, a member of the Dutch Everest expedition, climbed Changtse without a permit and against the wishes of his expedition leader. Contemporary Dutch accounts described him setting out alone after being ordered not to, returning later that day to announce success.

Changtse from the upper slopes of Lhakpa Ri. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

Eleven days after Taks’ unauthorized solo push, on October 14, 1982, the first official ascent of Changtse was achieved by members of a German party.

The German Alpine Club team, co-led by Eduard Geyer and Hansjuergen Tauscher, approached the mountain via the East Rongbuk route. The expedition included climbers Paul Braun, Thomas Dunsser, Martin Engler, Walter Ernst, Rudolf Frick, Andreas Heckmair Jr., Ludwig Hoesle, Peter Lechart, Udo Zehetleitner, and Wilfried Zink.

The team drove from Lhasa and established their Base Camp near the final moraine of the Rongbuk Glacier at 5,105m. From there, they pushed up Everest and Changtse without the help of high-altitude porters. The climbers relied on their own strength and a team of six yaks to establish Camp 1 at 5,601m on October 2, followed two days later by Camp 2 at 6,096m, at the foot of Changtse’s long northeast ridge.

To get higher, the climbers first had to climb a difficult 610m snow-and-ice slope mixed with exposed rock. They established Camp 3 at 6,400m, sheltered behind a protective rock spur. Above this point, they fixed ropes along a steep slope on a wide ridge that curved first north and then sloped east. On October 13, they successfully placed Camp 4 high on the ridge at 6,903m.

On October 14, Zehetleitner completed the first official ascent, climbing via the four-kilometer northeast ridge, starting from the junction of the East Rongbuk and Changtse Glaciers. Two days later, on October 16, Braun, Frick, Hoesle, and Engler also topped out. They listed Changtse’s height as 7,550m.

Everest and Changtse. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

In May 1983, the first Chilean expedition to Everest was already stretched thin by high altitude and extreme logistics when internal friction pushed the team over the edge. Among the climbers was 25-year-old glaciologist Gino Casassa, who had been temporarily sidelined by altitude sickness and was sent down to Base Camp to recover.

As his health improved, Casassa grew restless under the strict commands of his expedition leader, Gaston Oyarzun. Forbidden from taking unnecessary risks, Casassa instead fixed his sights on Changtse. At 3:30 am on May 14, Casassa secretly slipped out of camp alone, starting an unauthorized solo attempt up the mountain’s long northeast ridge — the same route used by the Germans.

Moving rapidly in the subzero darkness without a permit, radio communication, or backup, he gambled everything on a lightweight style. By 3:30 pm, he was just 10m below the summit. However, the upper sections of the ridge deteriorated into unstable snow cornices and deep powder. Casassa narrowly escaped disaster when the snowpack fractured and slumped 4.5m beneath his boots, threatening to trigger a massive avalanche down the face.

Refusing to retreat, Casassa bypassed the unstable ridge by traversing directly onto the steep, exposed north face. He finally reached the summit at 5:00 pm. After a difficult descent in the dark, he reached Camp 2 at 11:00 pm, exhausted and dehydrated.

Back at camp, his unexpected return sparked outrage rather than celebration. While Casassa was on the peak, his teammates were managing a high-altitude medical emergency, and his unauthorized disappearance had caused immense panic.

Because the climb lacked official Chinese permits, it also carried diplomatic risks for future Chilean expeditions. The Chilean Mountaineering Federation officially expelled Casassa, concluding one of the era’s most astonishing solo feats with immediate controversy.

In May 1986, a massive Chinese–Japanese expedition (17 Japanese and 19 Chinese climbers) targeted the mountain. After establishing an Advance Base at the confluence of the Changtse and East Rongbuk Glaciers, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier and the northeast ridge.

On May 10, 16 climbers reached the summit. Among them was Tibetan climber Gunsang (also spelled Guisang), who became the first woman to summit Changtse. A second wave of eight Chinese climbers topped out the following day, while the remaining Japanese climbers withdrew to assist a teammate suffering from high-altitude sickness. According to the Himalayan Database, Gunsang remains the only woman to summit.

Ed Webster’s photo on August 26, 1986, during his first attempt on Changtse’s Northeast Ridge. Two days later, he established a new route, solo via the Southeast Face. Photo: Ed Webster

Later that same summer, American mountaineer Ed Webster arrived to attempt a bold, lightweight climb.

On August 26, 1986, he initially turned back from 7,163m on the right side of the face because of dangerously thin snow over brittle shale. After just a single rest day, he launched another attempt on August 28 and established a landmark new route up the southeast face.

Starting from an Advance Base at 6,126m near the foot of the North Col, Webster climbed the lower, highly avalanche-prone sections in total darkness to capitalize on the stable nighttime freeze. He navigated a prominent snow gully between two massive rock buttresses, traversed the upper face, and connected with the German northeast ridge route to reach the summit alone in a 15-hour round trip.

In September 1987, an Australian expedition led by Robert Turner arrived at the East Rongbuk side of the mountain. On September 29, despite punishing high-altitude winds and deteriorating conditions, Turner and Glen Nash reached the summit. They climbed via a central couloir to the left of the north face icefall. This completed a line that was closely related to a route scouted by a Japanese team the previous year.

Changtse attracted global attention in late summer 2016 because of two remarkable solo ascents. Jordi Tosas of Spain reached the summit via the east ridge on August 27, and Kilian Jornet followed on September 11, via a variant line up the northeast face.

The total number of Changtse summits remains low, at around 60. The standard line remains the northeast ridge.

Illustrated photo of the 2016 expedition for the American Alpine Journal. From the approach to the north: (A) Point 6,822m; (B) Everest; and (C) Changtse. (1) Approach to the east ridge of Changtse (first ascent 1982). (2) Jornet variant on the north face (2016). (3) Japanese variant on the north face (1986). Photo: Jordi Tosas

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8556. Everest Climbers Return to West Ridge With One Member Less

On their second venture up Everest, the Russian team is aiming to progress further along the West Ridge. This time, they will be a team of just three: Natalya Belyankina was airlifted out yesterday due to health problems.

Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will climb one of the longest routes of Everest, with no supplemental oxygen, no support team, and no clear idea about the exact line they will follow.

Kondrashkin recently posted details about their previous ascent to the Lho La and the beginning of the ridge last week. As he noted, their route skirts below gigantic hanging seracs. They felt safe traversing the area on the way up because they saw no avalanche debris. However, after they reached the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide col, the boom of a falling serac below them reminded them of the risks.

On the following morning, the climbers approached the first part of the West Ridge.

“[It was] a sharp ascent to the ridge: first, on a 50˚ snow slope and, higher up, more than 100m of 60˚ glacial ice,” Kondrashkin recalled. “Then, climbing over a slight snow cornice, we emerged onto the ridge.”

Shipilov and Vasiliev climbed further up a rocky outcrop, looking for both the most suitable line and a potential campsite on the ridge. They also photographed the sections ahead. As Kondrashkin and Belyankina watched from below, “It felt like we were looking at it from the very foot of the mountain, just how enormous it is,” Kondrashkin wrote about Everest’s upper half:

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Serguey Kondrashkin

The team returned to Base Camp the following day, finding a better route that involves less time under the hanging seracs.

Since then, they have been resting and preparing for the next foray up. However, the rest was not enough for Natalya Belyankina, who was already suffering from a bad case of Khumbu cough.

Natalya Belyankina in the helicopter back to Kathmandu today. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

“It’s a real pity,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote today. “Natasha did so much to make this expedition happen, but it’s impossible to continue in this condition.”

Vasiliev then confirmed that Kondrashkin, Shipilov, and he are heading up again today for about a week.

The Russians are the only climbers currently on an 8,000m peak, and their goal is among the most ambitious on Everest in years. They intend to climb the mountain entirely on their own, without supplemental oxygen, in a light style, via the West Ridge.

On Pete Poston’s graph of Everest routes, the Yugoslavian route is #5 in pink, and the 1963 U.S. route is #2 in green.

The West Ridge of Everest has been climbed just three times, each via different variations, all of them epic and sometimes tragic expeditions. Climbing the West Ridge involves two possible routes. First, an endless climb along the ridge from Nepal like the 1979 Yugoslavian team did (Andrej Stremfelj, Nejc Zaplotnik, Stipe Bozic, Stane Belak-Srauf, and Ang Phu Sherpa).

Second, they could cross into Tibet at some point and continue up the North Face via the Hornbein Couloir. This route retraces the steps of Americans Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, who started up the normal route to Camp 2, then joined the West Ridge and crossed to what became known as the Hornbein Couloir to the summit in 1963.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

#8554. Alaska to Patagonia, One Summit at a Time

Since 1972, Alaska to Patagonia has been a classic cycling route of 30,000km or more. At any given time, several ambitious cyclists are attempting it. But no one is doing it quite like Tobias Renggli of Lucerne, Switzerland.

The 23-year-old endurance athlete is not only pedaling the distance but also climbing the highest peak in each of the 35 countries he passes through. And although it’s part of the marketing rather than the adventure, the imagery so far — shot both by Renggli and by a film production group he belongs to called the Black Forest Collective — is stunning for such a difficult journey.

Despite his age, this is not Renggli’s first adventure. In 2022, at the age of 18, he cycled all 44 European countries within seven months, climbing the highest peak of each and camping every night. In 2024, he climbed the highest mountains of all 26 Swiss cantons in about three weeks.

Renggli began in April from Deadhorse, Alaska, on the shores of the Beaufort Sea — still deep winter at that latitude, though the long Arctic days had returned. Pedaling 1,200km in temperatures as low as -30˚C, he made his way to Talkeetna, then skied in for eight days while pulling a sled.

He then summited 6,190m McKinley with his occasional partner, Heli Hofmann — the first party atop the peak this year, which meant they had to break trail through the deep snow. It took them 36 days.

Next, it was onto 5,959m Mount Logan, Canada’s highest peak. Again with Heli Hofmann but no guide, they summited in late June. This time, they were the last party of the year to summit Logan.

Renggli then cycled with another friend to Vancouver, took a two-week break after covering 3,000km and summiting two of the hardest peaks he would encounter, then continued alone through the U.S. Typically, he cycles 100 to 160km per day, with some shorter days.

Unlike most Trans-America cyclists, he chose to take Baja California rather than mainland Mexico. Crossing Baja was more difficult than expected. He described temperatures exceeding 40°C and a 120km stretch toward Loreto that he began with only two liters of water.

Later, near Ciudad Insurgentes, thunderstorms flooded the roads. At night, he carried his bicycle through a fast-moving, thigh-deep flood while vehicles turned back.

Renggli had intended to take no motorized transportation, only sailboats when confronted with water — he also wants to climb 12 high points in the Caribbean. However, this is such a massive undertaking that he’s not being too strict on himself. Although he skied into Denali, for example, he flew back out to Talkeetna. And from La Paz in Baja, he caught the ferry to Mazatlan on the mainland and continued from there.

Details have been sparse since Baja, but Renggli recently crossed into Guatemala. Presumably, he climbed 5,636m Pico de Orizaba before leaving Mexico and is now headed to 4,220m Volcán Tajumulco, Guatemala’s highest peak. He has been on the road for 202 days.

#8553. Australian Grandfather Attempts 1,650Km River Swim

Australian grain farm manager Scott Gladman, 63, is attempting to swim the length of the Darling River, Australia’s third-longest river. It begins in New South Wales and finishes at its confluence with the Murray River at Wentworth. Gladman believes he will be the first person to swim the entire 1,650km route.

Gladman started on September 1 from near Brewarrina in far north New South Wales. At the outset, he budgeted 103 days to complete the swim, averaging around 16km per day. So far, he is largely on track. After 49 days, he has covered 660km, leaving just under 1,000km to go.

Interestingly, the expedition is not born from a love of endurance swimming. Gladman was inspired to find a fundraising challenge to support friends impacted by Motor Neuron Disease and Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, a rare form of Parkinson’s. Initially, he considered the Murray. “I just thought I could swim the Murray River, but people have done that,” he told ABC News. “No one has had a crack at the Darling.”

The location of the Darling River in Australia. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Gladman gave himself 18 months to train. In the summer, he swam in the Murray River at Boundary Bend, Victoria, and during winter he completed laps in indoor pools. Now out on the Darling, a support boat of family and friends keeps him company, alongside a canoeist.

“There’s no real form of communication, and I wear earplugs…he’ll [the canoeist] either have to hit me on the back of the head with a paddle to get my attention, or he’ll just start steering toward me, and that will push me one way or the other,” Gladman said.

Despite its length, the Darling River is sometimes so shallow that Gladman needs to float through sections on his back, or walk. The support boat also sometimes requires saving, with Gladman having to help clear a path through river debris:

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. #8551. A Latte Every Workday Costs Over $1,000 a Year – Brew Most Cups at Home

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A coffee shop latte costs about $5, and buying one most workdays adds up to more than $1,000 a year. At home, the same drink costs about 70 cents. Make most cups yourself with a setup that pays for itself within two months, and keep a café visit or two a week as the treat.

That $5 is the typical price of a 12-ounce latte at independent coffee shops, according to the fall 2026 Coffee Price Index by Fresh Cup. Buy one five workdays a week for 50 weeks and that’s $1,250 a year, before tax and tip.

Making the latte yourself costs a fraction of that. Ground coffee averaged $9.25 a pound in October 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. At the weakest strength the National Coffee Association suggests for a French press, a 12-ounce mug takes about 22 grams of coffee, roughly 45 cents’ worth. Brew those 22 grams with less water for a strong base, add 8 ounces of whole milk at the bureau’s average of $4.10 a gallon, and a latte costs about 70 cents.

Pricier beans don’t close the gap. At $15 a pound, that latte costs about $1, still about $4 less than the café’s $5. Plain drip has a gap too, $3.25 for 12 ounces in those shops against about 45 cents at home.

The switch lasts only if you like the home cup, so spend on beans you enjoy before you spend on gear. A drip coffee maker or French press handles plain coffee. For lattes, pair a handheld milk frother with a moka pot, a stovetop brewer that makes strong, espresso-style coffee. Add a travel mug for the commute, plus a grinder if you buy whole beans, and keep the total near $100. At about $4.30 saved per homemade latte, that setup pays for itself in about 23 cups, six to eight weeks at three or four homemade lattes a week.

Judge any upgrade the same way. A $500 espresso machine takes about 117 homemade lattes to break even.

Keep the café for the visits you’d miss most. Brew at home three or four days a week, buy a latte on the others, and the year’s coffee costs about $390 to $610 instead of $1,250.

#8550. Seven Alpine-Style Climbs Happening Now in Nepal

Several small teams are attempting difficult climbs on Nepal’s 6,000 and 7,000m peaks. Unfortunately, they rarely report on their plans or progress until they return, and often only if they succeed.

This is what we know about the ongoing expeditions:

Three young French climbers, members of the Military High Mountain Group from Chamonix, celebrated their organization’s 50th anniversary with a new route on Peak 41. This 6,654m mountain is located in the Khumbu region and is often called the “true Mera Peak.”

Konrad Piontek, Amaury Fouillade, and Clovis Paulin took advantage of a good weather window and achieved the first ascent of the peak’s northeast face. They climbed in an alpine-style single push over four days. The result is a beautiful 1,400m line with difficulties up to ED+ 5+ M6 A1 90°. They descended via the southeast face. The team named their line Bon Matin (good morning).

Nivel Meroi and Romano Benet are acclimatized and ready to attempt a new route on Jugal II, but the Italian couple will be on their own. Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, has left due to illness.

Meanwhile, in the Kangchenjunga region, a large Russian team has also finished acclimatizing. The team trekked in the area and crossed a number of high-altitude passes, the latest of them at the top of an icefall at 5,750m. They reported lots of snow above 5,000m but are ready to attempt a new route on the formidable Jannu (7,710m) from its southeast side.

The team comprises Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin.

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan traveled to Nepal in September, aiming to achieve the first ascent of Gangapurna West (7,455m), also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal. They have provided no news since, but they probably had to retreat when an intense snowstorm hit the Annapurna region three weeks ago.

Location of Gangapurna West on a Google Earth screenshot. Notes by Lindsay Griffin for the American Alpine Journal.

Meanwhile, a second team has reached the base of the peak with the same objective. Valery Shamalo, Natalia Zanina, Maksim Trufanov, and Ruslan Kirichenko arrived at the beginning of October and saw no one else there. They reported that recent precipitation had left the trail in a poor state; the climbers had to cross landslides and swollen rivers to reach base camp.

The team has completed two acclimatization climbs, looking for a passage through the icefall at the base of the mountain and then a series of couloirs. They reached 5,900m and, on a second trip, 6,600m. Deep snow covered the peak, which slowed progress. Finally, they launched a summit bid last week.

From 6,600m, they spent a day on technical ice sections of 70–80º. In poor visibility, they endured spindrift and were showered by small ice chunks.

“In the afternoon, the weather deteriorated sharply,” Natalia Zanina said. “Heavy snowfall began, and we started being struck by large, continuous avalanches. At 6,800m (340m from the summit), we decided to turn back.”

A note on names: according to 8000ers.com, Asapurna should be the correct name for this peak because — although it is closer to Gangapurna — Asapurna’s summit ridge connects directly to Annapurna III.

The list of climbing permits granted by Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism points to some other interesting expeditions, some of them in remote western Nepal. There is a permit for Nyalu Kang (6,265m), only opened to foreign climbers in 2024 and reportedly unclimbed, and Ardang, summited once by Canadians Bryce Kendall and Sunny Twelker in 2019. Victor Saunders and Mick Fowler of the UK attempted Ardang last year.

#8549. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 20

As we pointed out last week, most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents that have come to light recently.

Chamois in France. Photo: Ludovic Laude/L’Est Republicain

A normally timid mountain ungulate has been attacking runners on the outskirts of Besançon in eastern France.

One victim, a 30-year-old woman jogger, was knocked unconscious and suffered a punctured shoulder and serious scalp wounds requiring stitches and staples. The incident occurred just a few hundred meters from the outskirts of the city.

“I didn’t hear it coming,” the woman, known only as Milena, told Le Monde. “I only had time to see its head 10 centimeters from me, and then, nothing, total blackout…”

The woman was unconscious for about five minutes.

Another runner had been attacked days earlier. The incidents occurred near La Chapelle des Buis. Wildlife authorities described the behavior as highly unusual and authorized the animal’s removal. The cause of its aggression remains unclear.

A 71-year-old Winter Garden, Florida fisherman, Steven Hamilton, was posing for a photograph with a fish when a large alligator lunged from the water, seized his leg, and pulled him into a pond.

Emergency crews responded, but the alligator refused to let go of his body, according to Fox News. By the time they released him and killed the alligator, Hamilton was dead. The medical examiner identified drowning and blunt-force injury to his left leg as causes of death, with alligator tooth marks on both sides of the leg.

Alligator attacks are rare but occur occasionally. According to the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, there have been a total of 500 alligator bites against humans since 1948, including 32 fatal encounters.

Vladimir Odulo, a fisherman from Primorye in Russia’s Far East, survived an attack by an Asiatic black bear, also known as a Himalayan bear.

The bear attacked while Odulo was fishing. He tried to defend himself with his fishing rod, but the animal knocked him into the water. Odulo continued fighting as it “beat his face like a boxer,” Russian media reported the fisherman saying. Suddenly, the bear stopped the attack and fled into the forest.

Odulo suffered several wounds and a serious eye injury, but survived. Doctors in Vladivostok were able to save his eyesight.

A venomous Caspian cobra, which now occurs high in Himachal Pradesh. Photo: Shutterstock

Two deaths in the Indian Himalaya have been attributed to Caspian cobras. Native to Central Asia, this venomous species has expanded its range eastward into the higher reaches of Himachal Pradesh. It now also occurs in Pakistan and Kashmir.

The first death occurred when a 40-year-old man accidentally stepped on a Caspian cobra while spraying an apple orchard. Wearing open-toed footwear, he sustained two bites on his leg. He was taken to a local faith healer before being shifted to the hospital, where he was declared dead, according to the Tribune of India.

In the second case, a 62-year-old man stepped on a snake while on his way to work and was bitten on the leg. He collapsed within half an hour and was taken to a health facility, where he died.

These fatalities occurred some time ago, but the report on them was published just this week in the journal Epidemiology International. The Caspian cobra generally inhabits higher, open, rocky terrain at elevations of 2,000m or higher, where both incidents occurred. Researchers suggest its range may now include lower elevations.

Two men died in separate elephant attacks in northern Kenya.

On October 11, Eisimgai Gorow Ltarakwa, 41, was herding goats near Nguposorogin village when a lone elephant attacked him. He suffered severe injuries and died at the scene.

Two days later, Mukhtar Abdoy Hussein, 64, was grazing livestock near Benane village when a herd of elephants trampled him to death.

The incident highlights the risks faced by herders in areas where livestock grazing activities bring communities into close proximity with wildlife. Under a conservation initiative, the families are entitled to receive compensation, according to Kenyan media.

#8548. A 76-Year-Old Kazakh Blacksmith Is Walking Around the World

Sarsenbay Kotyrashov had never left his native Kazakhstan when, in 2023, he set out to walk across the Caucasus. A blacksmith from the industrial province of Ulytau in central Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov had in tow only a battered suitcase and his signature leather hat as he crossed the Kazakh border. He was 73 years old.

Now, three years later, Kotyrashov has almost 30,000 followers on Instagram who have tuned in for his journeys on foot across Eurasia. People stop him and ask for selfies with Ulytauman, his online moniker and a reference to his home province.

Alongside his growing social media presence, Kotyrashov has been working with UNESCO to document Kazakh artisanal practices. He is now 76, and his travels are far from over.

Kotyrashov started his first job at age nine, working as a herder. By the time he entered his 70s, he had worked an astonishing diversity of manual labor jobs: carpenter, joiner, stonemason, lathe operator, metalworker, and most recently blacksmith. His expertise in traditional artisanship landed him a job at the Ulytau National Reserve Museum, a 150,000-hectare open-air museum comprising everything from mountains to mausoleums. From 2010 to 2020, Kotyrashov worked restoring historical buildings on the reserve, some of which date back to the Bronze Age.

The mausoleum of Jochi Khan, a 12th century Mongol ruler, is only one of the 25 building complexes at the Ulytau National Museum Reserve. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Tourists came from around the world to visit the reserve. Kotyrashov began to dream of traveling like them. “Why not?” he asked himself. “Why haven’t I seen the whole world myself? In my entire life, I’ve only ever seen Ulytau and Astana.”

Then came the pandemic, and his wife of 40 years passed away. Kotyrashov built a small hand-cart and set out across Kazakhstan on foot. “I chose to travel on foot, because when you walk, you notice much more, including nature, landscapes, animals, and plants,” he explained. “There is also time to think, to reflect, and to understand things.”

Kotyrashov’s first journey in 2022 was a love letter to Kazakhstan. As he walked from town to town over 181 days, pulling a homemade cart weighing around 60kg, he spoke with local artisans about their crafts. He tied a flag to his cart to promote the Qymyzmuryndyk festival, which celebrates the traditional Kazakh drink of kumis, or fermented mare’s milk. Local governments began holding press conferences for him and organizing lodging.

“Each day, I would meet with anywhere from 150 to 500 people in different parts of the country,” he told a Kazakh outlet. “The greatest discovery of my journey was the people — the citizens of Kazakhstan. They are generous, kind, noble, and open-hearted; I was truly struck by the kind of people who inhabit our Kazakhstan. It gives me hope for a better future.”

In 2023, he crossed the border into Russia, then followed the spine of the Caucasus Mountains through Chechnya and Georgia, and finally into Türkiye. Sometimes, he bivouacked in his sleeping bag. In towns, though, Chechen and Ingush Georgian locals invited him to stay with them. In Türkiye, he slept in mosques.

Kotyrashov decorated his cart with flags celebrating Kazakhstan. Photo: Kazinform

After his trip to Türkiye, Kotyrashov tackled China. Unlike in Central Asia and the Caucasus, he finally had to pay for hotels. By now, though, he had secured a trip coordinator and sponsors who helped him cover the costs. He took photos at the Great Wall and ended his journey in Beijing.

Europe posed greater difficulties. Everywhere else he had visited, he walked along the side of the highway. Unbeknownst to him when he began his 2026 trip, 3,000km from Belgrade to Paris, walking on highways is largely illegal in Europe. He had replaced his cart with an old suitcase, but the suitcase bit the dust on an unpaved footpath 150km outside Paris.

But Kotyrashov had an appointment. Determined to make it, he left the suitcase behind and sped on with his backpack.

On April 24th, he arrived at the UNESCO World Heritage Center in Paris and presented officials there with a handmade iron bell. At the Center, he met with Kazakhstan’s permanent UNESCO representative and shared his research on Kazakh artisanship and nomadic travel.

Kotyrashov on the Great Wall of China. Photo: Astana Times

After returning from Paris, Kotyrashov began working once more as a blacksmith to save up for his next trip. Sponsors help him with lodging and food, but he still needs to pay for his own gear. “Over the course of six months, I wore out seven pairs of shoes,” he said.

In 2027, he will set out to another continent: the Americas. He aims to cross the United States from coast to coast, starting in Florida and ending in California. After his experience in Europe, he’s studying up on American highway law.

Three years ago, Kotyrashov left Kazakhstan for the first time. Now, he’s hoping the American trip will contribute to his broader goal of claiming a Guinness record for the most miles walked by a person over 75.

“I had never traveled far in my life,” he said. “But it is never too late to travel.”

Year          Route                                                                                   Distance

2022      Across Kazakhstan, ending in Aktau on the Caspian Sea       ~8,000km

2023     Atyrau, Kazakhstan → Russia → Caucasus → Türkiye             ~3,000km

2024     Kazakhstan → Russian Altai → Mongolia → China                   uncertain

2026    Belgrade → Hungary → Austria → Germany → Paris                 ~3,000km

Rey’s other academic interests include astronomy during the French Revolution, US aerospace export controls, and 18th century charlatan physicist Johann Bessler.
