#8504. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8501. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8499. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8497. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8494. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8492. 10 Things I’m Dreading About Thru-Hiking the Appalachian Trail

I recently wrote about the 10 things I’m most excited about when it comes to thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail.

However, as any Appalachian Trail thru-hiker can tell you, the AT is a trail that throws a lot at you. As excited as I am to experience such an iconic trail culture, I am dreading some of the more uncomfortable aspects of the journey. So, before I willingly sign up for five months of relentless discomfort, here’s what I am dreading most about thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail.

Coming from the dry air of the West, the sheer humidity of the East Coast is a fear of mine. I know what it’s like to sweat, but I’m used to everything drying out overnight. There is a special kind of misery in waking up damp, packing away a wet tent, and immediately sweating through my clothes before I even start the first climb.

Drying gear out feels nearly impossible when the air itself feels wet, and I know I need to accept that I will seldom feel truly dry on this trail. That’s easy to write about from my comfortable couch; yet in practice, I fear that the persistent dampness will chip away at my mental fortitude more than I can currently anticipate.

Rain gear can only do so much. Photo via Katie Jackson

While the shade and lightning protection are comforting, I find the prospect of the AT’s endless Green Tunnel daunting. On other trails I’ve hiked, even the tree-covered sections would frequently open onto a high ridge or exposed pass that rewarded me with fantastic views. The AT’s canopy shelters hikers from their hard-earned views more than I’m used to, and I once again fear the mental toll of not seeing the vistas I love.

I know the answer is to learn to love the minute changes of the Green Tunnel, but that’s a big ask when I’m accustomed to walking through some of the grandest, most objectively stunning views in America. Will I be able to find a deeper motivation for a thru-hike other than seeing pretty places? Your guess is as good as mine.

The trees are beautiful, but after a while I want to see some MOUNTAINS! Photo via Katie Jackson

Ticks freak me out in a way I struggle to articulate. As someone with a deep fear of needles, something about looking down and seeing a bug with its head buried inside your skin makes the back of my neck itch. Even the concept of tick checks causes some anxiety; the possibility of finding a tick on me is as stressful as the creature itself.

To make matters worse, this isn’t a fear I can just tamp down and avoid. The consequences of leaving a tick attached can be severe. Lyme disease is on the rise in ticks found out East, along with a whole host of other tick-borne illnesses. The idea of having to perform a full-body tick check every single night adds a persistent, low-grade anxiety to camp life that I’ve never experienced on a trail before.

I’ll also throw snakes on this list. I’m not stoked by the number of venomous snakes out there. Photo via Katie Jackson

Western trails can be steep, technical, exposed, and rocky, but the long-distance trails are often graded with switchbacks and are designed for foot traffic. The AT, by contrast, frequently takes the most direct route up and down the mountains’ fall lines, and much of the trail is naturally composed of tree roots, mud pits, and slick rock.

My pace while hiking the Long Trail was slower than any long trail I’ve done before; to keep myself from falling on the challenging terrain, I sometimes had to slow down to nearly a crawl. This unpredictable terrain stresses my joints and muscles in a way that a clear singletrack doesn’t. I’ll be going into this trail with a persistent back injury, so I’m worried that five months of awkward steps will be a bit too much for my body to handle.

Not only is it very humid, but the trail itself doesn’t make it easy to stay dry. Photo via Katie Jackson

Even in the best of circumstances, I don’t sleep well on trails (or in normal life). One thing I do love about sleeping on thru-hikes is the total silence that comes with the backcountry. However, on the AT, I don’t expect to spend much time at all in the deep backcountry.

While the noise of nearby roads or towns isn’t the end of the world, I truly dread sharing shelters with the worst wildlife of all: snorers.

I know that hiker etiquette suggests choosing a different spot to sleep if you know yourself to be a snorer, but I’m also not naive enough to expect all hikers to follow that social contract. People suggest earplugs, but I’ve never found earplugs to actually block noise for me. Maybe I have oddly shaped ear canals, maybe I’m hypersensitive to the sound, or maybe I just haven’t found the right pair quite yet.

Either way, I worry that I will end up not able to utilize the convenience of the shelters because staying in one with a snorer will lead to a sleepless night.

Shelters seem so comfortable and convenient, but I know I need to prioritize being able to actually fall asleep. Photo via Katie Jackson

Hiking southbound means you are racing the calendar from day one, and as the weeks tick by, watching the daylight shrink is a constant stress. Out West, even when days get shorter in the fall, you usually have wide-open skies that let you stretch your hiking hours into the late dusk. Under the heavy canopy of the AT, once the sun starts dropping, the Green Tunnel goes pitch black in a hurry.

I’m not opposed to night hiking, but I don’t have a ton of experience with it. In order to meet the pace I’m hoping to keep on trail, I know I’ll have to get a lot more accustomed to it. That will either turn into a pleasant surprise as I learn I really love hiking after dark, or it’ll be a constant frustration.

The woods after dark can get a little spooky. Photo via Katie Jackson

While I love a trail town, the AT in particular seems like a trail that could suck me into a town and make it difficult to leave. Towns, I’ve found, are the single biggest cause of my spending on thru-hikes, so I want to try my best to avoid financial traps when possible. Hostels are unfortunately too comfortable and I love a meal from a restaurant too much to resist when I’m near one; and, on the AT, you’re always near one.

I don’t personally think that spending time in towns will affect my momentum or motivation, but I have a very specific amount of money saved for this hike and I fear for my budget. On the CDT, I spent less than $5,000 on my hike, largely by hitting the trail already in shape and minimizing my time in towns. On the AT, I worry that neither of these things will be possible for me.

I can’t help it! I love a side quest! Photo via Katie Jackson

I have never felt grosser than I did at the Northern Terminus of the CDT. Like many, I struggle to eat while hiking, especially if I’m trying to force down food I’m not thrilled about. Combined with the food desert that blankets much of that trail, I found myself eating pure junk for five months straight. By the end of the trail, my diet of Honey Buns and sticks of butter left me exhausted, poorly recovered, and craving a vegetable.

This is more of a general worry about thru-hiking than an AT-specific fear. This time around, I really want to force myself to eat better, but I worry I’ll run into the same problem with a lack of appetite. I’m not sure I can mentally or physically handle five more months of Little Debbie’s products, but I also know my body will need every calorie I can get my hands on.

I know I’m a generally stressed out person. Photo via Katie Jackson

While part of my affinity for cowboy camping stems from my laziness about setting up my tent, I truly love opening my eyes at night and seeing the wide expanse of stars in the sky with the Milky Way slashing across.

For so many reasons (bugs and rain), I know that frequent cowboy camping on the AT is generally a little less realistic. Even if I do choose to sleep out under the stars, the odds that I actually get a clear view of the sky through the trees feel low.

Even in the daytime, I’m massively attached to the wide-open sky sprawl of the West. I love seeing the weather roll in hours in advance. I love seeing glimpses of the trail miles away. Trading those sweeping views for something that feels a bit more sheltered and claustrophobic already makes me a little bit sad.

I love an open, expansive view. Photo via Katie Jackson

Opting to start southbound means beginning my hike in the relatively unforgiving Maine terrain. There is no gentle “ease in” period to build trail legs, such as what I had in New Mexico on the CDT. I’ll be thrown directly into some of the steepest and most technical terrain on the entire trail.

In my experience on the CDT, I felt physically the strongest near the middle but actually felt weaker and weaker as I hiked further into Montana and the hike started to wear on my body. Therefore, I’m trying to remind myself that Maine may be almost equally as challenging for me if I were to go NOBO; if my brain and body are exhausted from the culmination of the hike, I still won’t be in great shape to take on the climbs, even if I feel like I should be.

Still, knowing that the first week on trail will likely be a masterclass in physical suffering is a terrifying way to start a long journey.

I’ve done enough hiking in the White Mountains to know it won’t really get any easier after Maine. Photo via Katie Jackson

Pre-hike nerves are expected before a trail, or at least that’s what I keep telling myself.

I’ve loved every long trail I’ve had the privilege of hiking before, even the ones I didn’t expect to deeply love, so I’m excited to face these fears, figure out which ones don’t actually bother me at all, and work through the remainder while also discovering all the surprises about the trail that I love.

#8491. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8488. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8486. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8483. Andrew Skurka on Vapor Barrier Liners for Winter Camping

This article is adapted from Andrew Skurka’s first-person video for The Trek’s YouTube channel, part of a weekly series. Edited for clarity and readability.

On a multi-day winter backpacking trip, your own sweat can become one of your biggest problems. Moisture builds up in your gloves, boots, insulated jackets, and sleeping bag. When temperatures stay below freezing, drying everything out can be nearly impossible.

That’s where vapor barrier liners (VBLs) come in. These intentionally non-breathable layers keep perspiration from reaching your insulation. They can feel clammy and take some getting used to, but in the right conditions they can make a remarkable difference.

I learned this the hard way. I was the first person to complete the Sea-to-Sea Route, and during that trip I spent the winter on the trail, snowshoeing 1,400 miles through Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. In January 2007, a few months before the Great Western Loop, I hiked about 380 miles along Minnesota’s North Shore from Duluth to Ely, a trip I called Ultralight in the Nation’s Icebox. And I started the Alaska-Yukon Expedition in mid-March in Kotzebue, north of the Arctic Circle. I still remember that for the first three days, the temperature never got above 15 degrees below zero.

The Sea-to-Sea Route was my first legitimate winter backpacking experience, and I wore a pretty traditional layering system. It was basically an extension of what I’d wear in three-season conditions:

When I say cold, I mean daytime temperatures that never get above freezing, ideally no warmer than the 20s, and nighttime lows in the single digits or teens. The same problem applies at anything colder.

You’re active during the day. In the heat of the day, when it’s 20 degrees out and you’re really moving on snowshoes or skis, you might wear just a midweight base layer, or maybe you need a fleece. Either way, you’re perspiring from the activity. And at night, your body is still losing moisture through insensible perspiration.

If you’re wearing all of your layers at night inside a sleeping bag, that moisture moves out through your layering system. It usually gets trapped in my active insulated jacket, or on the inside of my waterproof-breathable shell, or, if I’m in my sleeping bag, inside my big arctic puffy. As the moisture moves away from your body, it gets colder and colder until it hits the dew point, and that point is often inside your layering system or inside your sleeping bag.

Even if you’ve never backpacked in winter, this has probably happened to you. After a day of alpine skiing at a resort, you notice the inside of your gloves is pretty wet. So is the inside of your plastic ski boots.

That’s not a problem if you’re out for the day, because you get home or into a hut and dry everything out. On a backpacking trip, you can’t. You can’t dry out your sleeping bag, your boots, your gloves, or your big belay parka, so the moisture stays trapped. All your stuff gets wet and stays wet, and when it’s wet, it’s also cold.

That was my failing on the Sea-to-Sea Route back in 2004 and 2005. I could go out for a night or two, but by nights three, four, and five, moisture was accumulating in my layers and my sleeping bag. After a couple of days out, I needed to get inside somewhere warm and dry so I could reset all of my systems and safely go out again.

A vapor barrier liner is a non-breathable layer worn just outside a thin or midweight base layer and underneath your insulating layers. The fluorescent orange jacket I’m wearing in the video is an example. Instead of allowing perspiration to move into your fleece, parka, or sleeping bag, the barrier keeps that moisture closer to your skin.

There’s a tradeoff: the sweat doesn’t magically disappear. It stays inside the barrier, where your base layer may become damp or clammy. That’s why I pay close attention to how hard I’m working, and I vent or adjust layers before I start sweating heavily.

If you’re considering multi-day backpacking or thru-hiking in winter with daytime temperatures consistently around 20°F or colder, I think vapor barrier liners are well worth looking into. They can significantly reduce the moisture buildup I just described, although they don’t replace good temperature management or protection from outside moisture.

With vapor barrier liners, your layering system looks like this:

For more on building a clothing system from a small set of versatile pieces, see The Only 12 Backpacking Clothes You Really Need.

The first benefit is that a vapor barrier liner protects your exterior layers. It keeps them warm by keeping them dry.

With the VBL on, I’m still perspiring a little, but much of that body moisture is stopped by the barrier instead of moving into my fleece or insulated parkas. At night, I can wear my insulating layers inside my sleeping bag while greatly reducing how much perspiration reaches the bag’s insulation. It won’t make my sleeping bag waterproof or eliminate every source of condensation, but it helps protect against moisture coming from my body.

If you’re wearing what’s almost a trash bag next to your skin, you’re going to be very aware of how much you’re perspiring, because it starts to feel clammy. When you feel that clamminess, it’s your sign to moderate your effort, so maybe you go slower, or to start taking layers off.

Sometimes you’re in between. You don’t want to take a layer off because you’re not that warm, but you definitely need to expel some heat and moisture. That’s when you ventilate. RBH Designs makes a fantastic vapor barrier outer layer, like the one I’m wearing, with all sorts of venting features: a full front zip, pit zips, and zippers on the arms. You can keep wearing the layer but really open it up so the heat and moisture escape.

In very cold weather, you don’t want a lot of ways to lose heat, which is why you carry lots of puffy layers and multiple layers. Without a vapor barrier liner, moisture moves through your layers, and as it gets close to the outside, it evaporates. That evaporation steals heat away from you. A VBL does an excellent job of keeping your heat next to you and preventing that evaporative heat loss.

Here’s a classic scenario that even three-season backpackers will relate to. You hike up a mountain without moderating your effort much. As you climb, it gets cooler and cooler, maybe you enter the clouds and lose the sun, and when you finally reach the top, your back is drenched and your hair is wet with sweat. Then, as you’re signing the summit register, you start getting cold, because all that sweat is evaporating off your body. A vapor barrier liner keeps that moisture inside. You can think of it as its own microclimate, so you don’t get that evaporative heat loss.

If you want to wander into vapor barrier liners, start with gloves. My layering system for really cold weather starts with the DeFeet Duraglove wool glove. It’s definitely a liner glove, but it has more heft than most. Over that, I go straight to the RBH Designs mitts.

When I notice my hands starting to get clammy from sweat, it’s easy. I take the mitt off and loop it onto a carabiner on my backpack’s shoulder strap. Then I can ski or snowshoe for a while without it, and when my hand starts to get cold again, I put the mitt back on.

Again, the idea with vapor barrier liners is that you become sensitive to your rate of perspiration, and you either moderate your effort or take off or adjust layers so that you sweat less.

With daytime temperatures no warmer than the teens, I would move toward vapor barrier liner socks. Here’s how the system works, from the inside out:

Then all of that goes into my boot. For those curious, mine are old-school leather three-pin telemark boots, where the telemark binding clamps down on the duckbill at the front.

Vapor barrier liner socks become important because otherwise the sweat from your feet gets into the outer layers of the boot, or gets trapped inside it, and then it’s tough to get the boot dry.

The very last thing you’d add to your vapor barrier liner system is a pair of vapor barrier liner pants. It has to be pretty cold to warrant them, with daytime highs in the low to mid teens and ideally in the single digits. Your legs generate so much heat that it has to be really cold before you’d want running tights with vapor barrier liner pants on top.

As with the top, you want the pants to be really well ventilated, maybe with full or three-quarter zips on the legs. That way you can easily open them up to let the heat and moisture out, and keep moving without having to take the pants off completely because you’re overheating and sweating too much.

With all the temperature ranges I’ve given you, keep in mind that they depend on the other conditions: how much sun there is, how much wind there is, and whether you’re walking on dirt, which absorbs a lot more solar radiation, or on ice or snow, which reflects the sun back at you. You might adjust these recommendations up or down for when to start using vapor barrier liners.

Vapor barrier clothing is a niche category, so you won’t find many options in mainstream backpacking stores. Rab makes vapor barrier socks, and Western Mountaineering offers a vapor barrier liner for sleeping bags.

For purpose-built VBL clothing, I recommend looking at RBH Designs. I’ve had excellent experiences with its equipment, including vapor barrier mitts, socks, and ventilated jackets. As with any specialized winter gear, check current availability and sizing before purchasing.

In addition to jackets, pants, socks, and mitts, there’s another commercially available option: a vapor barrier liner for your sleeping bag. You wear your base layer shirt, pants, and socks, then sleep inside the VBL, which goes inside your sleeping bag.

That’s an effective way to reduce perspiration getting into your sleeping bag’s down or synthetic insulation, because most of the body moisture stays inside the liner’s microclimate. It won’t, however, protect your sleeping bag from moisture coming from outside the liner.

My big hang-up with a vapor barrier sleeping bag liner is that you can’t use it during the day. You still end up with the same situation: you have on your liner gloves and a normal mountaineering mitt, your hands are sweating, and that sweat is making its way into the insulation of the mitt. That’s not going to help you on day two. I think it’s better to have vapor barrier liner technology not only at night, to keep your sleeping bag from getting wet, but also during the day, to keep your outer layers from getting wet.

What’s the minimum trip length where I’d want vapor barrier liners? My answer is anything of one night or more.

Suppose it’s a two-day, one-night trip, and it’s two full days. If you follow the conventional wisdom of using breathable layers, you have your liner gloves and a standard overmitt without a vapor barrier liner. At the end of the first day, your mitt is very wet and very cold. When you wake up in the morning and put it back on, it’s not going to be as nice to wear as it was on the first day.

With boots, you’re perspiring through your feet all day long, and that moisture gets trapped inside your boot. When you wake up in the morning, your boot is going to be frozen. I’ve done a lot of very uncomfortable things in the outdoors, but one of the most uncomfortable is putting your foot inside a frozen boot.

If you ever end up with wet shoes, either from your sweat or from external water like a creek crossing, the key is what you do when you pull into camp at night. Open up the shoe, really extend the tongue, and loosen the laces as much as you possibly can. Then just let it freeze overnight. In the morning, jam your feet inside, and the warmth of your feet will sort of thaw it out. If it freezes in that open position, you can at least get your feet into the shoe.

One additional advantage of using vapor barrier liners is that I can rely more confidently on down insulation during long winter trips. You don’t need VBLs to use down in winter, but limiting the body moisture that reaches it helps preserve its warmth over consecutive days.

You’ve probably heard the usual pros and cons of down versus synthetic insulation. Down generally offers more warmth for its weight. And while synthetic insulation tends to retain more warmth than down when damp, the idea that it stays fully warm when wet is misleading. Wet synthetic insulation still loses insulating performance, just usually not as much as wet down.

With a vapor barrier protecting my outer layers from perspiration, I can use a down sleeping bag, a down belay parka, and even a down active parka with less concern about that particular source of moisture. Those pieces are generally excellent for warmth-to-weight, and good down insulation can last for many years. My GoLite down belay parka dates back to 2009. A VBL doesn’t protect any of this gear from snow, rain, or other outside moisture, though, so keeping it dry still matters.

I’ve been talking about vapor barrier liners for a long time. I used them extremely successfully on Ultralight in the Nation’s Icebox in 2007 and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition in 2010. Yet in the last 15 or 20 years, the market hasn’t changed very much. There are a few good products out there, but the selection is still small.

That’s fine. I think there’s a very small market for vapor barrier liners because, let’s be honest, not many people go out in the wintertime on multi-day or multi-night trips. The days are short, the nights are long, it’s very cold, and it can be kind of lonely.

But winter can also be a beautiful time to be in the backcountry. It extends your season if you want to do more than backpack between June and September. It’s a way to expand your skill set, and you may learn things you can apply to your three-season trips. Getting out at all times of the year, not just when the weather’s nice, will definitely make you a better backpacker.

There’s not a lot of information out there about vapor barrier liners. I wrote a blog post about them years ago that now has more than 200 comments. If you have questions about vapor barrier liners, ask them in the comments on the video, and I’ll try to get to them.

On multi-day winter trips, body moisture can build up in your layers and sleeping bag night after night, and drying everything out may be impossible. A vapor barrier liner worn just outside your base layer reduces how much perspiration reaches your insulation, makes you more aware of when you’re sweating, and helps limit evaporative heat loss. I consider VBLs especially worthwhile when daytime temperatures stay around 20°F or colder: start with mitts, consider socks when highs are in the teens, and save pants for particularly cold conditions. Even for a single overnight trip in those conditions, they’re worth a serious look. You still need to manage your sweat and keep outside moisture off your gear.

Andrew Skurka has backpacked more than 30,000 miles and has been named Adventurer of the Year by both Outside and National Geographic. He is the author of The Ultimate Hiker’s Gear Guide and founded his guided backpacking program in 2011.

Skurka no longer guides winter trips, but his team leads guided backpacking trips in three-season conditions in southern Utah, the High Sierra, Alaska, and Yellowstone. The 2027 schedule will be posted by November 6, 2026, and applications open December 7, 2026.

#8480. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition plan includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#8475. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.
